Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 5, verse 105–109 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who have believed, upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾ – the verse. The scholars differed in the interpretation of this verse. Some of them left it to its apparent meaning.

Damrah ibn Rabi'ah said: al-Hasan recited this verse and said, "Praise be to God for it, and praise be to God for acting upon it. There has never been a believer in the past, nor a believer in what remains, except that beside him is a hypocrite who dislikes his deed."

Some of them said: its meaning is, ﴿upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾, so act in obedience to God; ﴿those who have gone astray will not harm you when you are guided﴾, that is, when you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.

Abu al-Bakhtari, from Hudhayfah, regarding this verse: "When you enjoin and forbid."

Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid narrated from Abu Zibyan, from Qays ibn Abi Hazim, who said: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may God be pleased with him) said from the pulpit: "You recite this verse, ﴿O you who have believed, upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾ – the verse – and you place it other than its proper place, and you do not know what it is. I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'When people see an evil and do not change it, God will surely encompass them with punishment. So enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and do not be deceived by God's words, ﴿O you who have believed, upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾, so that one of you says, "Upon me is my own self." By God, you must enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, or [else] the worst of you will be placed in authority over you; then the best of you will call upon God, but He will not answer them.'"

[Kanz al-'Ummal: 3/681, no. 8447 (similar in meaning).] It is indicated by the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: "We said, 'O Messenger of God, if we do not enjoin what is right and do not forbid what is wrong, until there remains no good except that we act upon it and no evil except that we refrain from it, and we never enjoin or forbid anyone again?'"

He (peace be upon him) said: "Enjoin what is right; if they do not accept all of it, [at least] they will not be forbidden from [what is] wrong entirely, and if they do not refrain from all of it..."

It was also said: the meaning of the verse is, ﴿upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾ when you have enjoined what is right and forbidden what is wrong, but it was not accepted from you.

Shaqiq ibn 'Uqbah said: It was said to Ibn 'Umar, "If you sat down in these days and did not enjoin or forbid, for God has said, ﴿upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves; those who have gone astray will not harm you when you are guided﴾."

Ibn 'Umar said: "It does not apply to me or to my companions, for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, 'Let the one present convey to the absent.' [Musnad Ahmad: 1/230.] So we were the present and you are the absent. But this verse is for people who will come after us, who, if they say [it], will have their words not accepted."

Sahl ibn al-Ashhab narrated from al-Husayn and al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah, that this verse was recited to Ibn Mas'ud, ﴿O you who have believed, upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾. Ibn Mas'ud said: "This is not its time. Say it [only] when it is accepted from you; when it is rejected by you, then upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves." Then he said: "The Qur'an was revealed when it was revealed: among it are verses whose interpretation has already passed; among it are verses whose interpretation occurred in the time of the Messenger of God; among it are verses whose interpretation will occur shortly after the Prophet (ﷺ); among it are verses that will occur and not be fulfilled after today; among it are verses that will occur at the end of time; and among it are verses whose interpretation will occur on the Day of Resurrection, such as what is mentioned of the reckoning, Paradise and Hell. So as long as your hearts and your desires are united, and you have not been divided into factions, and some of you have not tasted the violence of others, then enjoin and forbid. But when hearts and desires diverge, you are divided into factions, and some of you taste the violence of others, then it is each man for himself – and at that point the interpretation of this verse arrives."

Abu Umayyah al-Sam'ani said: I heard Abu Tha'labah [al-Khushani] about this verse, ﴿O you who have believed, upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾.

Abu Tha'labah said: "I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about it, and he said: 'Enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, until you see a religion being preferred, miserliness being obeyed, desire being followed, and every person of opinion being pleased with his own opinion; then take care of your own self and leave aside their common folk, for behind you are days of patience. Whoever acts in obedience to God in those days, the one who has gone astray and perished after him will not harm him, and the reward of the doer on that day will be like the reward of fifty doers of what you are upon.'" [al-Sunan al-Kubra of al-Bayhaqi: 10/92.] [123]

They said: "O Messenger of God, the reward of fifty doers from among them?" He said: "No, rather the reward of fifty doers from among you."

Some of them said: this verse was revealed concerning the people of desires.

Abu Ja'far al-Razi said: A young man from among the people of desires came to Safwan ibn Harith and mentioned something of his affair. Safwan said: "Shall I not direct you to the particular [mark] of God by which He distinguishes His friends: ﴿O you who have believed, upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾ – the verse." [Tafsir al-Tabari: 7/132.]

al-Dahhak said: ﴿upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾ when desires differ, so long as there is no sword or whip.

Ibn Jubayr said: this verse was revealed concerning the People of the Book, meaning, ﴿upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves; those who have gone astray will not harm you﴾ from among the People of the Book.

al-Kalbi narrated from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) wrote to the people of Hajar, whose governor was al-Mundhir ibn Sawi al-Tamimi, calling them to Islam; and whoever refused should pay the jizyah. When the letter reached him, he presented it to those with him from among the Jews, Arabs, Christians and Magians, and they acknowledged the jizyah but disliked Islam. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) wrote to him: "As for the Arabs, nothing is accepted from them except Islam or the sword; as for the People of the Book and the Magians, accept the jizyah from them." [Asbab al-Nuzul: 142; Zad al-Masir: 2/330.] [124] When the letter of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) was read to them, the Arabs embraced Islam, and the People of the Book and the Magians gave the jizyah. The hypocrites of Makkah said concerning this: "How strange! Muhammad claims that God sent him to fight people until they say, 'There is no god but God,' yet he accepted the jizyah from the Magians of Hajar and the People of the Book, and he has not compelled them to Islam, while he returned it to our Arab brothers?" This was very grievous to the Muslims, so God revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾, meaning: after the message has been delivered by Muhammad, so beware. And He revealed, after the Arabs had embraced Islam, ﴿There is no compulsion in religion; the right course has become distinct from error﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning all the disbelievers. That was because when a man embraced Islam, they would say, "You have made your father foolish, and you have gone astray, and you have done such and such." So God revealed: ﴿upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves; those who have gone astray from among your fathers will not harm you when you are guided﴾. This is an expression of urging, and the Arabs use such words as "'alayka" (upon you), "labbayka" (at your service), "ilayka" (to you), "'indaka" (with you) and "dunaka" (beside you). [See Tafsir al-Tabari: 7/138.]

Then He said: ﴿To God is your return, all of you﴾, the misguided and the guided, ﴿and He will inform you of what you used to do﴾.

﴿O you who have believed, testimony between you [is required] when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest – the verse﴾

It was revealed concerning three men who went out as merchants from Madinah to Syria: 'Adi ibn Fadi and Tamim ibn Aws al-Dari, both of them Christians, and Budayl, the freedman of 'Amr ibn al-'As al-Sahmi, who was a Muslim emigrant. They differed about the kunyah of his father.

al-Kalbi said: "Budayl ibn Abi Mazinah." Qatadah, Ibn Sirin and 'Ikrimah said: "He is Ibn Abi Mariyah," as did Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Yasar and Ibn Abi Maryam. When they reached Syria, Budayl fell ill and wrote a document containing everything he had with him, and placed it among his goods, without informing his companions. When his illness grew severe, he made a bequest to Tamim and 'Adi and instructed them to deliver his goods to his family when they returned. Budayl died, and they searched his goods and took from them a vessel of silver, engraved with gold, containing three hundred mithqal of silver adorned with gold. They concealed it, then completed their business, returned, and came to Madinah, and they delivered the goods to the family of the deceased. They searched [and found] the document, in which was listed everything he had, and they found that the vessel was missing from it, [namely] the silver vessel adorned with gold, weighing three hundred mithqal. They came to Tamim and 'Adi and said: "Did our companion sell any of his goods?" They said, "No." "Did he suffer a loss in trade?" They said, "No." "Did his illness last long so that he spent on himself?" They said, "No." They said, "We found in his goods a document in which was listed what he had, and we are missing from it a silver vessel adorned with gold, three hundred mithqal of silver." They said: "We do not know; he only bequeathed something to us and instructed us to deliver it to you, and we delivered it; we have nothing but what was decided." So they brought the matter to the Prophet (ﷺ), and God revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, testimony between you [is required] when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest: two just witnesses from among you﴾. [Tarikh Dimashq: 11/71.]

The people of Kufa said: its meaning is "let two witness," the wording of the verse being a report but its meaning an command. The people of Basra said: its meaning is "the testimony between you is the testimony of two," so the testimony was elided and the two were placed in its stead, like His saying, ﴿and ask the town﴾, meaning "ask the people of the town," and the town was placed in his stead and so put in the accusative.

Some of them said: its meaning is, "the testimony between you when death approaches one of you, that two should bear witness, [being] just, trustworthy and sound of mind, ﴿from among you﴾, O assembly of believers, from among the people of your religion and your community."

This was said by all the exegetes except 'Ikrimah and 'Ubaydah, who said: its meaning is "from the tribe of the one making the bequest."

They differed concerning the description of the two. Some people said: they are the two witnesses who bear witness to the bequest of the one making it.

Others said: they are the two executors. God intended to emphasize the matter, so He made the executor two. The evidence for this interpretation is that He followed it with His saying, ﴿you detain them after the prayer, and they swear by God﴾, and a witness is not bound by an oath; and because the verse was revealed concerning the two executors. According to this view, "testimony" means presence, as in your saying, "I witnessed so-and-so," meaning "I was present." God said, ﴿Were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub?﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 133] – the verse – and He said, ﴿and let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾. [Surah al-Nur: 2]

﴿or two others from outside your [community]﴾, that is, outside your religion. This is the view of Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ubaydah, Yahya ibn Ya'mar and Abu Mahjan, who said: "If they do not find two Muslims, let them bear witness with two disbelievers."

Shurayh said: "If a man is in a foreign land and finds no Muslim to witness his bequest, let him call a Jew, a Christian, a Magian, or a worshipper of idols – whichever disbeliever it is – and his testimony is permissible. The testimony of disbelievers against Muslims is not permissible except during travel, and it is not permissible during travel except in a bequest. If two Muslim men come and testify contrary to their testimony, the testimony of the Muslims is accepted and the testimony of the disbelievers is nullified."

It is related from al-Sha'bi: a man from among the Muslims was overtaken by death and made a bequest, but he found no one from among the Muslims to witness his bequest. al-Ash'ari said: "This is a matter that had not occurred in the time of the Messenger of God." So he made them swear and upheld their testimony.

Others said: its meaning is "from outside your tribe and your clan." This is the view of al-Hasan, al-Zuhri and 'Ikrimah, who said: the testimony of a disbeliever is not permissible, whether in travel or at home.

﴿If you are travelling in the land﴾, that is, you journey and travel in the land, ﴿and the calamity of death befalls you﴾, and you make a bequest to them both and deliver your property to them, ﴿and they are not trusted [regarding] the rights of the heirs﴾, so they are suspected in that matter and the heirs accuse them of betrayal. Then the ruling in that case is ﴿you detain them﴾, that is, you stop them ﴿after the prayer﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: this is connected to His saying, ﴿or two others from outside your [community]﴾, from among the disbelievers. As for when the two are Muslims, there is no oath upon them.

They differed about what this prayer is. al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: it is after the 'Asr prayer. al-Suddi said: it is after the prayer of the people of their religion and community, because they do not regard the 'Asr prayer. ﴿and they swear by God﴾, that is, they swear, ﴿if you doubt﴾, that is, if you have doubts: ﴿We will not exchange it for any price﴾, meaning: we will not swear falsely by God for the sake of worldly gain that we would take on account of it, ﴿even if he were a near relative﴾, even if the one for whom we swear were a near relative of ours, ﴿and we will not conceal the testimony of God﴾. al-Sha'bi recited, "we will not conceal testimony of God" with tanwin, and "God" with a kasrah on the ha' by attachment, meaning "by God" as an oath. It is related from Abu Ja'far, "testimony of Allah" with the alif cut and its initial vowel kasrah, meaning "and we will not conceal testimony," then he began an oath, saying, "Allah," i.e., "by God" [...] [an illegible word] [...] with tanwin on the testimony, "Allah" with the alif and lam and a kasrah on the ha', making the interrogative a particle of oath. It is related from some of them, "testimony" with tanwin, "Allah" with a fathah on the ha', meaning "and we will not conceal the testimony of God." Otherwise, ﴿indeed we would then be among the sinners﴾.

When this verse was revealed upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he performed the 'Asr prayer and summoned 'Adi and Tamim, and they were made to swear beside the pulpit by God, besides whom there is no god, that they had not betrayed anything of what had been entrusted to them. He swore to that, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) let them go once they had sworn. Then they concealed the vessel for as long as God willed them to conceal it, and then it came to light. They differed about how the vessel came to light.

Ibn Jubayr related from Ibn 'Abbas that the vessel was found in Makkah, and they said: "We bought it from 'Adi and Tamim."

Others said: when the time passed, the vessel was made public, and this reached the Banu Tamim, so they came to the two about it. They said: "We had indeed bought this from them." They said: "Did you not both claim that our companion had sold nothing of his goods?" They said: "We did not have its price, so we disliked acknowledging it to you, and therefore we concealed it from you." So they brought them both before the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and God revealed:

﴿Then if it becomes known﴾, that is, it is discovered and comes to light. The root of "ʿathar" is falling upon or stumbling over something, and from it is the saying, "I stumbled upon such-and-such" when I struck it and fell upon it.

al-A'mash said:

"With a she-camel of firm stride, when she stumbles, / a fall is nearer to her than my saying 'ah'."

By his saying "'athart" he means: she struck the tip of her hoof on a stone or something else. Then it is used for everything that one comes upon unexpectedly after it had been hidden, as in their proverbs: "He stumbled upon the yarn at the last moment, so he left not a monkey in Najd."

﴿that they both﴾, meaning the two executors, ﴿have incurred sin﴾, that is, they have deserved sin by their false oaths and their betrayal. ﴿then two others from among the heirs of the deceased﴾ will ﴿stand in their place﴾, meaning in place of the two executors, ﴿from among those who have a claim﴾.

Ḥasan and Ḥafs read it with a fatḥah on the tā', and this is the reading of 'Ali and Ubayy ibn Ka'b, meaning "the one who has become due" – "ḥaqqa" and "istaḥqqa" have the same meaning. He said: ﴿al-awlayān﴾ refers back to "two others," "the two more deserving," and it was not made nominative by "istiḥqāq."

The rest read it with a ḍammah on the tā' in the passive, meaning those about whom and for whose sake the sin was incurred, namely the heirs of the deceased; the two swearers incurred guilt on their account and concerning them, according to the sense, as in His saying, ﴿over the kingdom of Solomon﴾.

Ṣakhr al-Ghayy said:

"Whenever you deny it, you will know it, / upon its edges is a sturdy, oozing [brand]."

﴿al-awlayān﴾ in the dual is read by most of the people of Kufa, and it is Ya'qub's preference, meaning "from among the first ones."

Ḥasan read "al-awwalūn," and the others read "al-awlayān" according to the dialect of "the others" (the second). That is permissible because "al-awwalān" is definite, while "al-ākharān" [is definite] by frequency, since when He said "from among those who" and made them two and described them, it became like a definite in meaning.

﴿They swear by God: "Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony"﴾, that is, by God, our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, meaning our oath is more worthy than their oath. Its parallel is His saying, in the matter of li'an, ﴿then the testimony of each of them is four testimonies﴾ [Surah al-Nur: 6], meaning oaths. This is like the speaker's saying, "I testify by God" and "I swear by Him." ﴿and we have not transgressed﴾ in our oath; ﴿indeed we would then be among the wrongdoers.﴾

When this verse was revealed, 'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Muttalib ibn Wada'ah al-Sahmi stood up and swore by God once after the 'Asr prayer, and the cup was handed over to them and to the heirs of the deceased. Tamim al-Dari, after he had embraced Islam and pledged allegiance to the Prophet (ﷺ), used to say: "God, mighty and majestic, has spoken truly: I took the cup, and so I repent to God and seek His forgiveness."

The oath passed to the two heirs because the two executors were proven to have possessed the vessel, then they claimed they had bought it. Likewise, if an executor claims that the one making the bequest bequeathed something to him and there is no evidence; and likewise if a man claims against another man a sum of money, and the defendant acknowledges that, then claims that he bought it from the claimant or that the claimant gifted it to him. In these cases and their like, it is ruled that the oath be returned to the claimant.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Abu al-Nadr, from Badhan, freed slave of Umm Hani, from Ibn Abbas, from Tamim al-Dari, who said: "We sold the cup for a thousand dirhams, and I and 'Adi divided it. When I embraced Islam, I felt guilty about that, after I had sworn falsely. I went to the heirs of the deceased and informed them that my companion had a similar amount. They rushed at him and brought him to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he asked them for evidence, but they found none. So he ordered the heirs to swear, and 'Amr and al-Muttalib swore. Then the five hundred was taken from 'Adi, and I returned the five hundred."

[See Tafsir al-Tabari: 7/156.]

This is His saying, ﴿That is more suitable that they should bring the testimony in its proper form﴾. That is, that is more fitting and more appropriate for the two executors to bring the testimony in its proper form, and likewise for all people, when they fear that the oaths will be returned and the rights imposed upon them.

﴿And fear God and listen﴾, and so on. The scholars differed concerning the ruling of this verse. Some of them said: it is abrogated (mansukh), and this was narrated from Ibn Abbas. Others said: it is muhkam (not abrogated), and this is the correct view.

﴿On the day﴾, that is, remember and beware, the day when ﴿God will gather the messengers﴾, and this is the Day of Resurrection, ﴿and say, "What was your answer?"﴾, that is, what did your peoples answer you, and what did your nations reject from you, when you called them to My monotheism and My obedience? ﴿They will say﴾, that is, they will say, ﴿"We have no knowledge."﴾ Ibn Abbas said: "We have no knowledge, except the knowledge that You know better than us."

Ibn Jurayj said: the meaning of His saying "What was your answer?" is: what did they carry, and did they believe after you, so that they would say, "We have no knowledge."

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, and al-Suddi, among those who say this: on that day they will be terrified and confused and will be unable to answer; then, after their minds return to them, they will bear witness concerning their nations.

So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) wrote to him: "As for the Arabs, nothing is accepted from them except Islam or the sword; as for the People of the Book and the Magians, accept the jizyah from them." The hypocrites of Makkah said concerning this: "How strange! Muhammad claims that God sent him to fight people until they say, 'There is no god but God,' yet he accepted the jizyah from the Magians of Hajar and the People of the Book, and he has not compelled them to Islam, while he returned it to our Arab brothers?" This was very grievous to the Muslims, so God revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾, meaning: after the message has been delivered by Muhammad, so beware. And He revealed, after the Arabs had embraced Islam, ﴿There is no compulsion in religion; the right course has become distinct from error﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning all the disbelievers. That was because when a man embraced Islam, they would say, "You have made your father foolish, and you have gone astray, and you have done such and such." So God revealed: ﴿upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves; those who have gone astray from among your fathers will not harm you when you are guided﴾. This is an expression of urging, and the Arabs use such words as "'alayka" (upon you), "labbayka" (at your service), "ilayka" (to you), "'indaka" (with you) and "dunaka" (beside you). [See Tafsir al-Tabari: 7/138.]

Then He said: ﴿To God is your return, all of you﴾, the misguided and the guided, ﴿and He will inform you of what you used to do﴾.

﴿O you who have believed, testimony between you [is required] when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest – the verse﴾

It was revealed concerning three men who went out as merchants from Madinah to Syria: 'Adi ibn Fadi and Tamim ibn Aws al-Dari, both of them Christians, and Budayl, the freedman of 'Amr ibn al-'As al-Sahmi, who was a Muslim emigrant. They differed about the kunyah of his father.

al-Kalbi said: "Budayl ibn Abi Mazinah." Qatadah, Ibn Sirin and 'Ikrimah said: "He is Ibn Abi Mariyah," as did Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Yasar and Ibn Abi Maryam. When they reached Syria, Budayl fell ill and wrote a document containing everything he had with him, and placed it among his goods, without informing his companions. When his illness grew severe, he made a bequest to Tamim and 'Adi and instructed them to deliver his goods to his family when they returned. Budayl died, and they searched his goods and took from them a vessel of silver, engraved with gold, containing three hundred mithqal of silver adorned with gold. They concealed it, then completed their business, returned, and came to Madinah, and they delivered the goods to the family of the deceased. They searched [and found] the document, in which was listed everything he had, and they found that the vessel was missing from it, [namely] the silver vessel adorned with gold, weighing three hundred mithqal. They came to Tamim and 'Adi and said: "Did our companion sell any of his goods?" They said, "No." "Did he suffer a loss in trade?" They said, "No." "Did his illness last long so that he spent on himself?" They said, "No." They said, "We found in his goods a document in which was listed what he had, and we are missing from it a silver vessel adorned with gold, three hundred mithqal of silver." They said: "We do not know; he only bequeathed something to us and instructed us to deliver it to you, and we delivered it; we have nothing but what was decided." So they brought the matter to the Prophet (ﷺ), and God revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, testimony between you [is required] when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest: two just witnesses from among you﴾. [Tarikh Dimashq: 11/71.]

The people of Kufa said: its meaning is "let two witness," the wording of the verse being a report but its meaning an command. The people of Basra said: its meaning is "the testimony between you is the testimony of two," so the testimony was elided and the two were placed in its stead, like His saying, ﴿and ask the town﴾, meaning "ask the people of the town," and the town was placed in his stead and so put in the accusative.

Some of them said: its meaning is, "the testimony between you when death approaches one of you, that two should bear witness, [being] just, trustworthy and sound of mind, ﴿from among you﴾, O assembly of believers, from among the people of your religion and your community."

This was said by all the exegetes except 'Ikrimah and 'Ubaydah, who said: its meaning is "from the tribe of the one making the bequest."

They differed concerning the description of the two. Some people said: they are the two witnesses who bear witness to the bequest of the one making it.

Others said: they are the two executors. God intended to emphasize the matter, so He made the executor two. The evidence for this interpretation is that He followed it with His saying, ﴿you detain them after the prayer, and they swear by God﴾, and a witness is not bound by an oath; and because the verse was revealed concerning the two executors. According to this view, "testimony" means presence, as in your saying, "I witnessed so-and-so," meaning "I was present." God said, ﴿Were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub?﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 133] – the verse – and He said, ﴿and let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾. [Surah al-Nur: 2]

﴿or two others from outside your [community]﴾, that is, outside your religion. This is the view of Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ubaydah, Yahya ibn Ya'mar and Abu Mahjan, who said: "If they do not find two Muslims, let them bear witness with two disbelievers."

Shurayh said: "If a man is in a foreign land and finds no Muslim to witness his bequest, let him call a Jew, a Christian, a Magian, or a worshipper of idols – whichever disbeliever it is – and his testimony is permissible. The testimony of disbelievers against Muslims is not permissible except during travel, and it is not permissible during travel except in a bequest. If two Muslim men come and testify contrary to their testimony, the testimony of the Muslims is accepted and the testimony of the disbelievers is nullified."

It is related from al-Sha'bi: a man from among the Muslims was overtaken by death and made a bequest, but he found no one from among the Muslims to witness his bequest. al-Ash'ari said: "This is a matter that had not occurred in the time of the Messenger of God." So he made them swear and upheld their testimony.

Others said: its meaning is "from outside your tribe and your clan." This is the view of al-Hasan, al-Zuhri and 'Ikrimah, who said: the testimony of a disbeliever is not permissible, whether in travel or at home.

﴿If you are travelling in the land﴾, that is, you journey and travel in the land, ﴿and the calamity of death befalls you﴾, and you make a bequest to them both and deliver your property to them, ﴿and they are not trusted [regarding] the rights of the heirs﴾, so they are suspected in that matter and the heirs accuse them of betrayal. Then the ruling in that case is ﴿you detain them﴾, that is, you stop them ﴿after the prayer﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: this is connected to His saying, ﴿or two others from outside your [community]﴾, from among the disbelievers. As for when the two are Muslims, there is no oath upon them.

They differed about what this prayer is. al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: it is after the 'Asr prayer. al-Suddi said: it is after the prayer of the people of their religion and community, because they do not regard the 'Asr prayer. ﴿and they swear by God﴾, that is, they swear, ﴿if you doubt﴾, that is, if you have doubts: ﴿We will not exchange it for any price﴾, meaning: we will not swear falsely by God for the sake of worldly gain that we would take on account of it, ﴿even if he were a near relative﴾, even if the one for whom we swear were a near relative of ours, ﴿and we will not conceal the testimony of God﴾. al-Sha'bi recited, "we will not conceal testimony of God" with tanwin, and "God" with a kasrah on the ha' by attachment, meaning "by God" as an oath. It is related from Abu Ja'far, "testimony of Allah" with the alif cut and its initial vowel kasrah, meaning "and we will not conceal testimony," then he began an oath, saying, "Allah," i.e., "by God" [...] [an illegible word] [...] with tanwin on the testimony, "Allah" with the alif and lam and a kasrah on the ha', making the interrogative a particle of oath. It is related from some of them, "testimony" with tanwin, "Allah" with a fathah on the ha', meaning "and we will not conceal the testimony of God." Otherwise, ﴿indeed we would then be among the sinners﴾.

When this verse was revealed upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he performed the 'Asr prayer and summoned 'Adi and Tamim, and they were made to swear beside the pulpit by God, besides whom there is no god, that they had not betrayed anything of what had been entrusted to them. He swore to that, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) let them go once they had sworn. Then they concealed the vessel for as long as God willed them to conceal it, and then it came to light. They differed about how the vessel came to light.

Ibn Jubayr related from Ibn 'Abbas that the vessel was found in Makkah, and they said: "We bought it from 'Adi and Tamim."

Others said: when the time passed, the vessel was made public, and this reached the Banu Tamim, so they came to the two about it. They said: "We had indeed bought this from them." They said: "Did you not both claim that our companion had sold nothing of his goods?" They said: "We did not have its price, so we disliked acknowledging it to you, and therefore we concealed it from you." So they brought them both before the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and God revealed:

﴿Then if it becomes known﴾, that is, it is discovered and comes to light. The root of "ʿathar" is falling upon or stumbling over something, and from it is the saying, "I stumbled upon such-and-such" when I struck it and fell upon it.

al-A'mash said:

"With a she-camel of firm stride, when she stumbles, / a fall is nearer to her than my saying 'ah'."

By his saying "'athart" he means: she struck the tip of her hoof on a stone or something else. Then it is used for everything that one comes upon unexpectedly after it had been hidden, as in their proverbs: "He stumbled upon the yarn at the last moment, so he left not a monkey in Najd."

﴿that they both﴾, meaning the two executors, ﴿have incurred sin﴾, that is, they have deserved sin by their false oaths and their betrayal. ﴿then two others from among the heirs of the deceased﴾ will ﴿stand in their place﴾, meaning in place of the two executors, ﴿from among those who have a claim﴾.

Ḥasan and Ḥafs read it with a fatḥah on the tā', and this is the reading of 'Ali and Ubayy ibn Ka'b, meaning "the one who has become due" – "ḥaqqa" and "istaḥqqa" have the same meaning. He said: ﴿al-awlayān﴾ refers back to "two others," "the two more deserving," and it was not made nominative by "istiḥqāq."

The rest read it with a ḍammah on the tā' in the passive, meaning those about whom and for whose sake the sin was incurred, namely the heirs of the deceased; the two swearers incurred guilt on their account and concerning them, according to the sense, as in His saying, ﴿over the kingdom of Solomon﴾.

Ṣakhr al-Ghayy said:

"Whenever you deny it, you will know it, / upon its edges is a sturdy, oozing [brand]."

﴿al-awlayān﴾ in the dual is read by most of the people of Kufa, and it is Ya'qub's preference, meaning "from among the first ones."

Ḥasan read "al-awwalūn," and the others read "al-awlayān" according to the dialect of "the others" (the second). That is permissible because "al-awwalān" is definite, while "al-ākharān" [is definite] by frequency, since when He said "from among those who" and made them two and described them, it became like a definite in meaning.

﴿They swear by God: "Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony"﴾, that is, by God, our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, meaning our oath is more worthy than their oath. Its parallel is His saying, in the matter of li'an, ﴿then the testimony of each of them is four testimonies﴾ [Surah al-Nur: 6], meaning oaths. This is like the speaker's saying, "I testify by God" and "I swear by Him." ﴿and we have not transgressed﴾ in our oath; ﴿indeed we would then be among the wrongdoers.﴾

When this verse was revealed, 'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Muttalib ibn Wada'ah al-Sahmi stood up and swore by God once after the 'Asr prayer, and the cup was handed over to them and to the heirs of the deceased. Tamim al-Dari, after he had embraced Islam and pledged allegiance to the Prophet (ﷺ), used to say: "God, mighty and majestic, has spoken truly: I took the cup, and so I repent to God and seek His forgiveness."

The oath passed to the two heirs because the two executors were proven to have possessed the vessel, then they claimed they had bought it. Likewise, if an executor claims that the one making the bequest bequeathed something to him and there is no evidence; and likewise if a man claims against another man a sum of money, and the defendant acknowledges that, then claims that he bought it from the claimant or that the claimant gifted it to him. In these cases and their like, it is ruled that the oath be returned to the claimant.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Abu al-Nadr, from Badhan, freed slave of Umm Hani, from Ibn Abbas, from Tamim al-Dari, who said: "We sold the cup for a thousand dirhams, and I and 'Adi divided it. When I embraced Islam, I felt guilty about that, after I had sworn falsely. I went to the heirs of the deceased and informed them that my companion had a similar amount. They rushed at him and brought him to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he asked them for evidence, but they found none. So he ordered the heirs to swear, and 'Amr and al-Muttalib swore. Then the five hundred was taken from 'Adi, and I returned the five hundred."

[See Tafsir al-Tabari: 7/156.]

This is His saying, ﴿That is more suitable that they should bring the testimony in its proper form﴾. That is, that is more fitting and more appropriate for the two executors to bring the testimony in its proper form, and likewise for all people, when they fear that the oaths will be returned and the rights imposed upon them.

﴿And fear God and listen﴾, and so on. The scholars differed concerning the ruling of this verse. Some of them said: it is abrogated (mansukh), and this was narrated from Ibn Abbas. Others said: it is muhkam (not abrogated), and this is the correct view.

﴿On the day﴾, that is, remember and beware, the day when ﴿God will gather the messengers﴾, and this is the Day of Resurrection, ﴿and say, "What was your answer?"﴾, that is, what did your peoples answer you, and what did your nations reject from you, when you called them to My monotheism and My obedience? ﴿They will say﴾, that is, they will say, ﴿"We have no knowledge."﴾ Ibn Abbas said: "We have no knowledge, except the knowledge that You know better than us."

Ibn Jurayj said: the meaning of His saying "What was your answer?" is: what did they carry, and did they believe after you, so that they would say, "We have no knowledge."

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, and al-Suddi, among those who say this: on that day they will be terrified and confused and will be unable to answer; then, after their minds return to them, they will bear witness concerning their nations.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 5, verse 105–109 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who have believed, upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾ – the verse. The scholars differed in the interpretation of this verse. Some of them left it to its apparent meaning.

Damrah ibn Rabi'ah said: al-Hasan recited this verse and said, "Praise be to God for it, and praise be to God for acting upon it. There has never been a believer in the past, nor a believer in what remains, except that beside him is a hypocrite who dislikes his deed."

Some of them said: its meaning is, ﴿upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾, so act in obedience to God; ﴿those who have gone astray will not harm you when you are guided﴾, that is, when you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.

Abu al-Bakhtari, from Hudhayfah, regarding this verse: "When you enjoin and forbid."

Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid narrated from Abu Zibyan, from Qays ibn Abi Hazim, who said: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may God be pleased with him) said from the pulpit: "You recite this verse, ﴿O you who have believed, upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾ – the verse – and you place it other than its proper place, and you do not know what it is. I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'When people see an evil and do not change it, God will surely encompass them with punishment. So enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and do not be deceived by God's words, ﴿O you who have believed, upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾, so that one of you says, "Upon me is my own self." By God, you must enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, or [else] the worst of you will be placed in authority over you; then the best of you will call upon God, but He will not answer them.'"

[Kanz al-'Ummal: 3/681, no. 8447 (similar in meaning).] It is indicated by the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: "We said, 'O Messenger of God, if we do not enjoin what is right and do not forbid what is wrong, until there remains no good except that we act upon it and no evil except that we refrain from it, and we never enjoin or forbid anyone again?'"

He (peace be upon him) said: "Enjoin what is right; if they do not accept all of it, [at least] they will not be forbidden from [what is] wrong entirely, and if they do not refrain from all of it..."

It was also said: the meaning of the verse is, ﴿upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾ when you have enjoined what is right and forbidden what is wrong, but it was not accepted from you.

Shaqiq ibn 'Uqbah said: It was said to Ibn 'Umar, "If you sat down in these days and did not enjoin or forbid, for God has said, ﴿upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves; those who have gone astray will not harm you when you are guided﴾."

Ibn 'Umar said: "It does not apply to me or to my companions, for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, 'Let the one present convey to the absent.' [Musnad Ahmad: 1/230.] So we were the present and you are the absent. But this verse is for people who will come after us, who, if they say [it], will have their words not accepted."

Sahl ibn al-Ashhab narrated from al-Husayn and al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah, that this verse was recited to Ibn Mas'ud, ﴿O you who have believed, upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾. Ibn Mas'ud said: "This is not its time. Say it [only] when it is accepted from you; when it is rejected by you, then upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves." Then he said: "The Qur'an was revealed when it was revealed: among it are verses whose interpretation has already passed; among it are verses whose interpretation occurred in the time of the Messenger of God; among it are verses whose interpretation will occur shortly after the Prophet (ﷺ); among it are verses that will occur and not be fulfilled after today; among it are verses that will occur at the end of time; and among it are verses whose interpretation will occur on the Day of Resurrection, such as what is mentioned of the reckoning, Paradise and Hell. So as long as your hearts and your desires are united, and you have not been divided into factions, and some of you have not tasted the violence of others, then enjoin and forbid. But when hearts and desires diverge, you are divided into factions, and some of you taste the violence of others, then it is each man for himself – and at that point the interpretation of this verse arrives."

Abu Umayyah al-Sam'ani said: I heard Abu Tha'labah [al-Khushani] about this verse, ﴿O you who have believed, upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾.

Abu Tha'labah said: "I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about it, and he said: 'Enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, until you see a religion being preferred, miserliness being obeyed, desire being followed, and every person of opinion being pleased with his own opinion; then take care of your own self and leave aside their common folk, for behind you are days of patience. Whoever acts in obedience to God in those days, the one who has gone astray and perished after him will not harm him, and the reward of the doer on that day will be like the reward of fifty doers of what you are upon.'" [al-Sunan al-Kubra of al-Bayhaqi: 10/92.] [123]

They said: "O Messenger of God, the reward of fifty doers from among them?" He said: "No, rather the reward of fifty doers from among you."

Some of them said: this verse was revealed concerning the people of desires.

Abu Ja'far al-Razi said: A young man from among the people of desires came to Safwan ibn Harith and mentioned something of his affair. Safwan said: "Shall I not direct you to the particular [mark] of God by which He distinguishes His friends: ﴿O you who have believed, upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾ – the verse." [Tafsir al-Tabari: 7/132.]

al-Dahhak said: ﴿upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾ when desires differ, so long as there is no sword or whip.

Ibn Jubayr said: this verse was revealed concerning the People of the Book, meaning, ﴿upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves; those who have gone astray will not harm you﴾ from among the People of the Book.

al-Kalbi narrated from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) wrote to the people of Hajar, whose governor was al-Mundhir ibn Sawi al-Tamimi, calling them to Islam; and whoever refused should pay the jizyah. When the letter reached him, he presented it to those with him from among the Jews, Arabs, Christians and Magians, and they acknowledged the jizyah but disliked Islam. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) wrote to him: "As for the Arabs, nothing is accepted from them except Islam or the sword; as for the People of the Book and the Magians, accept the jizyah from them." [Asbab al-Nuzul: 142; Zad al-Masir: 2/330.] [124] When the letter of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) was read to them, the Arabs embraced Islam, and the People of the Book and the Magians gave the jizyah. The hypocrites of Makkah said concerning this: "How strange! Muhammad claims that God sent him to fight people until they say, 'There is no god but God,' yet he accepted the jizyah from the Magians of Hajar and the People of the Book, and he has not compelled them to Islam, while he returned it to our Arab brothers?" This was very grievous to the Muslims, so God revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves﴾, meaning: after the message has been delivered by Muhammad, so beware. And He revealed, after the Arabs had embraced Islam, ﴿There is no compulsion in religion; the right course has become distinct from error﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning all the disbelievers. That was because when a man embraced Islam, they would say, "You have made your father foolish, and you have gone astray, and you have done such and such." So God revealed: ﴿upon you is [the responsibility for] yourselves; those who have gone astray from among your fathers will not harm you when you are guided﴾. [See Tafsir al-Tabari: 7/138.]

Then He said: ﴿To God is your return, all of you﴾, the misguided and the guided, ﴿and He will inform you of what you used to do﴾.

So he made them swear and upheld their testimony.

Others said: its meaning is "from outside your tribe and your clan." This is the view of al-Hasan, al-Zuhri and 'Ikrimah, who said: the testimony of a disbeliever is not permissible, whether in travel or at home.

﴿If you are travelling in the land﴾, that is, you journey and travel in the land, ﴿and the calamity of death befalls you﴾, and you make a bequest to them both and deliver your property to them, ﴿and they are not trusted [regarding] the rights of the heirs﴾, so they are suspected in that matter and the heirs accuse them of betrayal. Then the ruling in that case is ﴿you detain them﴾, that is, you stop them ﴿after the prayer﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: this is connected to His saying, ﴿or two others from outside your [community]﴾, from among the disbelievers. As for when the two are Muslims, there is no oath upon them.

They differed about what this prayer is. al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: it is after the 'Asr prayer. al-Suddi said: it is after the prayer of the people of their religion and community, because they do not regard the 'Asr prayer. ﴿and they swear by God﴾, that is, they swear, ﴿if you doubt﴾, that is, if you have doubts: ﴿We will not exchange it for any price﴾, meaning: we will not swear falsely by God for the sake of worldly gain that we would take on account of it, ﴿even if he were a near relative﴾, even if the one for whom we swear were a near relative of ours, ﴿and we will not conceal the testimony of God﴾. al-Sha'bi recited, "we will not conceal testimony of God" with tanwin, and "God" with a kasrah on the ha' by attachment, meaning "by God" as an oath. It is related from Abu Ja'far, "testimony of Allah" with the alif cut and its initial vowel kasrah, meaning "and we will not conceal testimony," then he began an oath, saying, "Allah," i.e., "by God" [...] [an illegible word] [...] with tanwin on the testimony, "Allah" with the alif and lam and a kasrah on the ha', making the interrogative a particle of oath. It is related from some of them, "testimony" with tanwin, "Allah" with a fathah on the ha', meaning "and we will not conceal the testimony of God." Otherwise, ﴿indeed we would then be among the sinners﴾.

When this verse was revealed upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he performed the 'Asr prayer and summoned 'Adi and Tamim, and they were made to swear beside the pulpit by God, besides whom there is no god, that they had not betrayed anything of what had been entrusted to them. He swore to that, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) let them go once they had sworn. Then they concealed the vessel for as long as God willed them to conceal it, and then it came to light. They differed about how the vessel came to light.

Ibn Jubayr related from Ibn 'Abbas that the vessel was found in Makkah, and they said: "We bought it from 'Adi and Tamim."

Others said: when the time passed, the vessel was made public, and this reached the Banu Tamim, so they came to the two about it. They said: "We had indeed bought this from them." They said: "Did you not both claim that our companion had sold nothing of his goods?" They said: "We did not have its price, so we disliked acknowledging it to you, and therefore we concealed it from you." So they brought them both before the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and God revealed:

﴿Then if it becomes known﴾, that is, it is discovered and comes to light. The root of "ʿathar" is falling upon or stumbling over something, and from it is the saying, "I stumbled upon such-and-such" when I struck it and fell upon it.

al-A'mash said:

"With a she-camel of firm stride, when she stumbles, / a fall is nearer to her than my saying 'ah'."

By his saying "'athart" he means: she struck the tip of her hoof on a stone or something else. Then it is used for everything that one comes upon unexpectedly after it had been hidden, as in their proverbs: "He stumbled upon the yarn at the last moment, so he left not a monkey in Najd."

﴿that they both﴾, meaning the two executors, ﴿have incurred sin﴾, that is, they have deserved sin by their false oaths and their betrayal. ﴿then two others from among the heirs of the deceased﴾ will ﴿stand in their place﴾, meaning in place of the two executors, ﴿from among those who have a claim﴾.

Ḥasan and Ḥafs read it with a fatḥah on the tā', and this is the reading of 'Ali and Ubayy ibn Ka'b, meaning "the one who has become due" – "ḥaqqa" and "istaḥqqa" have the same meaning. He said: ﴿al-awlayān﴾ refers back to "two others," "the two more deserving," and it was not made nominative by "istiḥqāq."

The rest read it with a ḍammah on the tā' in the passive, meaning those about whom and for whose sake the sin was incurred, namely the heirs of the deceased; the two swearers incurred guilt on their account and concerning them, according to the sense, as in His saying, ﴿over the kingdom of Solomon﴾.

Ṣakhr al-Ghayy said:

"Whenever you deny it, you will know it, / upon its edges is a sturdy, oozing [brand]."

﴿al-awlayān﴾ in the dual is read by most of the people of Kufa, and it is Ya'qub's preference, meaning "from among the first ones."

Ḥasan read "al-awwalūn," and the others read "al-awlayān" according to the dialect of "the others" (the second). That is permissible because "al-awwalān" is definite, while "al-ākharān" [is definite] by frequency, since when He said "from among those who" and made them two and described them, it became like a definite in meaning.

﴿They swear by God: "Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony"﴾, that is, by God, our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, meaning our oath is more worthy than their oath. Its parallel is His saying, in the matter of li'an, ﴿then the testimony of each of them is four testimonies﴾ [Surah al-Nur: 6], meaning oaths. This is like the speaker's saying, "I testify by God" and "I swear by Him." ﴿and we have not transgressed﴾ in our oath; ﴿indeed we would then be among the wrongdoers.﴾

When this verse was revealed, 'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Muttalib ibn Wada'ah al-Sahmi stood up and swore by God once after the 'Asr prayer, and the cup was handed over to them and to the heirs of the deceased. Tamim al-Dari, after he had embraced Islam and pledged allegiance to the Prophet (ﷺ), used to say: "God, mighty and majestic, has spoken truly: I took the cup, and so I repent to God and seek His forgiveness."

The oath passed to the two heirs because the two executors were proven to have possessed the vessel, then they claimed they had bought it. Likewise, if an executor claims that the one making the bequest bequeathed something to him and there is no evidence; and likewise if a man claims against another man a sum of money, and the defendant acknowledges that, then claims that he bought it from the claimant or that the claimant gifted it to him. In these cases and their like, it is ruled that the oath be returned to the claimant.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Abu al-Nadr, from Badhan, freed slave of Umm Hani, from Ibn Abbas, from Tamim al-Dari, who said: "We sold the cup for a thousand dirhams, and I and 'Adi divided it. When I embraced Islam, I felt guilty about that, after I had sworn falsely. I went to the heirs of the deceased and informed them that my companion had a similar amount. They rushed at him and brought him to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he asked them for evidence, but they found none. So he ordered the heirs to swear, and 'Amr and al-Muttalib swore. Then the five hundred was taken from 'Adi, and I returned the five hundred."

[See Tafsir al-Tabari: 7/156.]

This is His saying, ﴿That is more suitable that they should bring the testimony in its proper form﴾. That is, that is more fitting and more appropriate for the two executors to bring the testimony in its proper form, and likewise for all people, when they fear that the oaths will be returned and the rights imposed upon them.

﴿And fear God and listen﴾, and so on. The scholars differed concerning the ruling of this verse. Some of them said: it is abrogated (mansukh), and this was narrated from Ibn Abbas. Others said: it is muhkam (not abrogated), and this is the correct view.

﴿On the day﴾, that is, remember and beware, the day when ﴿God will gather the messengers﴾, and this is the Day of Resurrection, ﴿and say, "What was your answer?"﴾, that is, what did your peoples answer you, and what did your nations reject from you, when you called them to My monotheism and My obedience? ﴿They will say﴾, that is, they will say, ﴿"We have no knowledge."﴾ Ibn Abbas said: "We have no knowledge, except the knowledge that You know better than us."

Ibn Jurayj said: the meaning of His saying "What was your answer?" is: what did they carry, and did they believe after you, so that they would say, "We have no knowledge."

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, and al-Suddi, among those who say this: on that day they will be terrified and confused and will be unable to answer; then, after their minds return to them, they will bear witness concerning their nations.

When God said, "O Jesus, son of Mary," meaning when God said, "O Jesus son of Mary." The position of ʿĪsā is accusative (naṣb) because it is a vocative (nidāʾ) if you treat the phrase as one vocative. If you prefer to make it two vocatives, then ʿĪsā is in the nominative (rafʿ) because it is a single, unmodified vocative, and "ibn" is in the accusative because it is a vocative with an attached noun. The sense of the sentence is "O Jesus, O son of Mary." Its parallel is the line of poetry:

*O Ḥakam ibn al-Mundhir ibn al-Jārūd,*
*you are the generous, son of the generous, son of generosity.* [[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 3/448.]]

This is under the same rule of nominative and accusative, and "ibn al-Mundhir" is not exempt from the accusative.

﴿Remember My favor upon you﴾. Al-Ḥasan said: Remembering a favor is giving thanks for it. By His words "My favor" He means "My favors," the word being singular in form but plural in meaning, as in His words: ﴿If you should count the favor of God, you could not enumerate it﴾ [Qur'an 14:34]. He means "the favors of God," because counting does not apply to a single favor. ﴿Upon you, O Jesus, and upon your mother, Mary.﴾ Then He mentions the favors: ﴿When I supported you with the Holy Spirit﴾, that is, I strengthened you and helped you with the Holy Spirit, meaning Jibrīl (Gabriel). ﴿You spoke to the people in the cradle and in maturity﴾, as a child and as a grown man, a prophet. ﴿And when I taught you the Book﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: God sent him when he was thirty years old, and he remained in his mission for thirty months, then God raised him to Himself. [Zad al-Masir of Ibn al-Jawzi: 1/332.]

﴿And the Book﴾ means writing (al-khaṭṭ), ﴿and wisdom﴾ means knowledge and understanding, ﴿and the Torah and the Gospel﴾. ﴿And when you shape from clay﴾, to make, form, depict and measure, up to His words ﴿So blessed is God, the best of creators﴾ [Qur'an 23:14], that is, the best of those who shape from clay, ﴿like the form of a bird﴾, like the image of a bird.

﴿By My permission, and you breathe into it, and it becomes a bird by My permission﴾, alive, flying by My permission. ﴿And you heal the blind and the leper by My permission﴾. ﴿And when you bring the dead out﴾ from their graves, alive, ﴿by My permission﴾. He revived Sām ibn Nūḥ, two men, a woman and a girl. ﴿And when I restrained the Children of Israel from you﴾, that is, the Jews, when they resolved to kill you. ﴿When you came to them with clear proofs﴾, meaning the signs and miracles I have mentioned. ﴿Those among them who disbelieved said: "This is nothing but evident magic"﴾ [Qur'an 5:110], meaning what came to them of clear proofs. Whoever reads "sāḥir" (magician) with an alif, the pronoun refers to Jesus, peace be upon him.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥamdūn, Makkī ibn ʿAbdān, Abū al-Azhar, from Asbāṭ, from Mujāhid ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmayr, who said: When God said to Jesus, "Remember My favor upon you," he wore wool and ate leaves, did not store anything for tomorrow, had no house that could be ruined, and no child that could die. Wherever night overtook him, he spent it there.

﴿And when I inspired the disciples﴾, that is, I caused them to know and cast inspiration into their hearts. Inspiration (waḥy) has several kinds: inspiration in the sense of sending Jibrīl to the Messenger; inspiration in the sense of inner conviction, like the inspiration to the mother of Moses and to the bee; and inspiration in the sense of dreams, both while awake and asleep.

Abū ʿUbayda said: "awḥā lahā" means "awḥā ilayhā" (he inspired to her). The poet said:

*And who gives her firm standing, so she became steady,*
*and fastened her with the firm mountains?* [[Lisan al-ʿArab: 15/380; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 20/149.]]

Meaning: she was commanded. "Ilā" is a complement; it is said "awḥā" and "waḥḥā." God said: ﴿Because your Lord has inspired her﴾ [Qur'an 99:5]. Al-ʿAjjāj said:

*He inspired to her the settling, so she settled.*

That is, He commanded her to settle, so she settled. The ḥawāriyyūn (disciples) were the special companions of Jesus.

Al-Ḥasan said they were launderers. Mujāhid said they were hunters. Al-Suddī said they were sailors. [See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 4/97.] Qatāda said the ḥawāriyyūn were ministers. ʿIkrima said they were the chosen ones. They were twelve men: Buṭrus (Peter), Yaʿqūb (James), Yaḥnas, Andrawāsī, Khaylibs, Abrithalmā, Matta, Tūmās (Thomas), Yaʿqūb ibn Ḥalqiyā, Tadāwusays, Fatāṭiyā, and Tūdūs. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 6/20.] ﴿That you believe in Me and My Messenger﴾, meaning Jesus. They said, when they met them and joined them: ﴿We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾ [Qur'an 5:111].

﴿When the disciples said: "O Jesus son of Mary, can your Lord send down to us a table from heaven?"﴾ [Qur'an 5:112].

ʿAlī, ʿĀʾisha, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jubayr and Mujāhid read "hal tastaṭīʿu" with the ta' (you), and "rabbaka" with a fatḥa on the bā'. This is the choice of al-Kisāʾī and Abū ʿUbayd, meaning "can you ask your Lord," as in His words ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Qur'an 12:82]. They said that the disciples were not doubting the power of God. The rest read "yastaṭīʿu" with the yā' and "rabbuka" with a ḍamma on the bā'. It was said that they did not doubt the power of God, but the meaning is "will He send down or not," just as a man says to his companion, "Can you rise with me?" while he knows he is able, but he means "will you do it or not." Some took it literally, saying: some people erred, and they had walked, so Jesus said to them, in astonishment at their words: ﴿Can your Lord...?﴾ ﴿Fear God, if you are believers﴾, that is, lest you doubt the power of God, or attribute to Him incapacity or deficiency, and you are not believers.

Al-māʾida is the table on which food is placed. It is a form of an active participle, since it gives and feeds. Like their saying: māda yamīdu, ghāra yaghīru, and imtāda (he took hold), from which the verse of Ruʾba:

*Guiding the heads of the wealthy rivals*
*to the Commander of the Believers, the one who begs.*

That is, the one who seeks charity. Ruʾba said: al-māʾida is that which feeds, gives, and the eaters eat. The food is also called māʾida on the table, because it is eaten on the table, as they say of rain: samāʾ, and of fat: thaḥ.

The people of Kufa said: it was called māʾida because it makes the eaters sway (tamīdu), that is, incline. From this is His word: ﴿And He cast firm mountains upon the earth lest it sway with you﴾ [Qur'an 16:15]. The poet said:

*The killing of al-Kināni after him troubled me,*
*and the spacious earth nearly swayed under me.* [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 6/367.]]

The people of Basra said: it is an active form with the meaning of a passive, that is, it sways with those who eat from it, like His word ﴿a pleasing life﴾ [Qur'an 69:21], meaning a pleasing one.

Jesus answered them: ﴿Fear God, if you are believers﴾, so do not doubt His power. It was also said: ﴿Fear God﴾ lest you ask Him for something that the nations before you did not ask.

﴿They said: "We only want to eat from it"﴾, we seek certainty of His power. ﴿And that our hearts may be at rest﴾, that they may be calm. ﴿And that we may know that you have spoken truly to us﴾, that you are the Messenger of God. ﴿And that we may be among its witnesses﴾ [Qur'an 5:113], witnessing to God's oneness and power and to your prophethood and mission. It was also said: ﴿And be among its witnesses﴾ to you before the Children of Israel when we return to them.

﴿Jesus said then: "O God, our Lord, send down to us a table from heaven, to be a festival for the first of us and the last of us, and a sign from You; and provide for us, for You are the best of providers"﴾ [Qur'an 5:114]. ﴿A festival﴾ (ʿīd): the word "takūn" here is a state (ḥāl) moving to the future, meaning "being," as in His words ﴿so grant me from Yourself an heir who will inherit me﴾ [Qur'an 19:5-6], meaning one who will confirm me, according to the reading of the one who reads it in the nominative (raf').

ʿAbd Allāh (Ibn Masʿūd) and al-Aʿmash read "takun lanā" in the jussive (jazm), as the answer to a supplication.

ʿĪd is the name for what returns to you from anything. It is said: the festival days, al-fiṭr and al-aḍḥā, are ʿīd because they return every year. It is also said: "the pleasant phantom is an ʿīd." The poet said:

*O ʿīd, what is wrong with you of longing and a glow,*
*and a phantom that passes over the frightening nights at night?* [[Lisan al-ʿArab: 3/318.]]

Another said:

*Your heart has been accustomed from your forehead to a return;*
*a split has rent you, and you flee from it.*

Al-Farrāʾ recited:

*Alas for my liver, from the burning of love and passion,*
*when my heart has been accustomed to the festival of Umayma.*

Its root is ʿawd (with waw), because it comes from ʿāda yaʿūdu (to return). The waw was changed to yāʾ because of the kasra before it, like nayrān, mīqāt and mīʿād.

Al-Suddī said: it means we take the day it was sent down as a festival, which we and those after us venerate. Sufyān said: we pray on it. Al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad said: the ʿīd is every gathering day, as if they returned to it. Ibn al-Anbārī said: the ʿīd was called ʿīd because it is a return from sorrow to joy, so it is a day of happiness for all creatures. Do you not see that prisoners are not pursued or punished, wild animals and birds are not hunted, and children are not sent to school? [See Rawḍat al-Waʿiẓīn of al-Fattāl al-Nīsābūrī: 352.] It was also said: it was called ʿīd because every person returns to the rank of his station. Do you not see the difference in their clothes, conditions and actions? Some honor and some are honored, some oppress and some show mercy. It was also said: it was called so because it is a noble and excellent day, likened to the ʿīd, which is a noble, generous stallion known among the Arabs; they attribute to it, saying "ibil ʿīdiyya" (camels of ʿīd). [See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 6/368.] Al-Rāʿī said:

*A festival by which they folded upon their sighs,*
*folded like bridges, having descended in descent.* [[Lisan al-ʿArab: 4/325.]]

His words ﴿for the first of us and the last of us﴾ mean for those before our time and for those who will come after us.

Zayd ibn Thābit read "li-awwalinā wa-ākhirinā" in the plural. Ibn ʿAbbās said: it means we eat from it, the last of people as the first of them ate.

﴿And a sign from You﴾, a proof and argument. ﴿And provide for us, and You are the best of providers﴾ [Qur'an 5:114]. God said, answering Jesus: ﴿I am sending it down to you﴾ [Qur'an 5:115], meaning the table.

The people of Syria, Medina, Qatāda and ʿĀṣim read "munazziluhā" with the doubled zāy, because it was sent down repeatedly, and the form tafʿʿal indicates frequency, time after time, as in His words ﴿and We sent it down in gradual revelation﴾ [Qur'an 17:106].

The rest read it with the single zāy, as in His words ﴿Send down to us﴾. ﴿Then whoever among you disbelieves after that﴾ [Qur'an 5:115], that is, after the table was sent down, so they were transformed into apes and swine.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿImrān said: the most severely punished people on the Day of Resurrection are the hypocrites, those who disbelieved among the people of the table, and the people of Pharaoh.

The scholars differed about whether the table was actually sent down to them or not. Mujāhid said: the table was not sent down, and this is a parable God struck. Al-Ḥasan said: By God, no table was sent down. When the people heard the condition and were told ﴿Whoever among you disbelieves after that﴾, they sought forgiveness and said: "We do not want it, and have no need of it," so it was not sent down. But the correct view is that it was sent down, because of His words: ﴿I am sending it down to you﴾, and His report does not admit doubt. Reports have come in mass transmission (tawātur) from the Messenger of God ﷺ, his companions, the Successors and other scholars of religion, that it was sent down. Kaʿb said: It was sent down on Sunday, and for that reason the Christians took it as a festival.

They differed about its description and how it was sent down and what was on it.

Qatāda narrated from Jalās ibn ʿAmr, from ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, from the Messenger of God ﷺ, who said: "The table was sent down as bread and meat, because they asked Jesus for food they could eat that would not run out. It was said to them: 'It will remain for you as long as you do not betray, hide, or store. If you do that, I will punish you.' Their day had not passed before they hid, stored, and betrayed." [Hadith with its chain as given above.]

Isḥāq ibn ʿAbd Allāh said: some of them stole from it, and said: "Perhaps it will never come down again," so it was lifted up, and they were transformed into apes and swine.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: Jesus son of Mary said to the Children of Israel: "Fast thirty days, then ask God for whatever you wish and He will give it to you." They fasted thirty days, and when they finished they said: "O Jesus, if we worked for someone and completed his work, he would feed us a meal, and we would be satisfied from our hunger. So pray to God that He send down to us a table from heaven." Then the angels came down with a table they carried, on which were seven loaves and seven fishes, until they set it before them, and the last of people ate from it as the first of them did.

ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib narrated from Bādhān and Maysara, who said: whenever the table was set before the Children of Israel, hands from heaven competed over them with every food except meat.

Ibn Jubayr said from Ibn ʿAbbās: every kind of thing was sent down on the table except bread and meat.

ʿAṭāʾ said: every kind of thing was sent down on it except fish and meat.

al-ʿAwfī said: a fish came down from heaven with the taste of everything in it.

ʿAmmār and Qatāda said: it was a table coming down from heaven, and on it were fruits of Paradise.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: God sent down loaves of barley and fish. It was said to Wahb: "Would that not be enough for them?" He said: "No, it was not enough, but God weakened the blessing for them, so they ate and went out, and others came and ate, until they all ate from it and there was surplus."

Al-Kalbī and Muqātil said: God answered Jesus, peace be upon him: ﴿I am sending it down to you﴾ as you asked. "Whoever eats of that food and then does not believe, I will make him an example and a curse upon those after them." They said: "We are satisfied." Jesus called Shamʿūn, who was the most excellent of the disciples, and said: "Do you have food?" He said: "Yes, with me are two small fish and six loaves." He said: "Bring them to me." Jesus cut them into small pieces, then said: "Sit in a garden, in groups, each group of ten." Then Jesus stood and prayed to God, and God answered him, and blessing came down into it, and it became sound bread and sound fish. Then Jesus stood and began to place in each group what his fingers made, then said: "Eat, in the name of God." The food kept increasing until it reached their knees, and they ate what God willed, and there was surplus of five baskets, while the people numbered five thousand and more.

Everyone said: "We bear witness that you are His servant and His Messenger." Then they asked a second time, and Jesus prayed, and God sent down bread, fish, five loaves and two fish, and he did with them what he had done the first time. When they returned to their villages and told this story, those who had not witnessed it laughed at them and said: "Woe to you, it is only magic that has bewitched your eyes." Whoever God wished good for, He made him steadfast in his insight, and whoever He wished to test, He returned to his disbelief. So they were transformed into swine, with no child or woman among them. They remained like that for days, then died, and they left no offspring, did not eat, and did not drink. Thus is every transformed creature.

Kaʿb al-Aḥbār said: an inverted table came down from heaven, carried by angels between heaven and earth, on which was every food except meat.

Qatāda said: it used to descend on them morning and evening wherever they were, like the manna and the quails for the Children of Israel.

Yamān ibn Riʾāb said: they ate from it whatever they wished.

ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ narrated from Salmān al-Fārisī, who said: "By God, Jesus, peace be upon him, never followed any of the filth, never rebuked anything, never laughed aloud, never brushed flies from his face, never wiped his nose on anything, and never complained about anything. When the disciples asked him to send down the table, he wore wool and wept and said: ﴿O God, our Lord, send down to us a table from heaven﴾ [Qur'an 5:114], and ﴿provide for us, and You are the best of providers﴾. Then God sent down a red tablecloth between two clouds, one cloud above it and one cloud beneath it, while they looked at it [it came rising], until it fell from their hands. Jesus wept and said: ﴿O God, make me among the thankful. O God, make it a mercy and not a punishment and a curse.﴾"

The Jews looked at something they had never seen, and they found no fragrance better than its fragrance. Jesus said: "Which of you is best in works, so that he uncovers it, mentions the name of God, and eats from it?"

Shamʿūn, the leader of the disciples, said: "You are more deserving of that than we are." Jesus stood, performed ablution, prayed a long prayer, and wept much. Then he uncovered the cloth and said: "In the name of God, best of providers." Behold, a grilled fish, without its bones or thorns, dripping with fat; at its head was salt, and its tail stretched out with vinegar. Its face had all kinds of herbs except leeks, and there were five loaves, one with olives, the second with honey, the third with ghee, the fourth with cheese, and the fifth with dried meat.

Shamʿūn said: "O Spirit of God, is this from the food of this world or from the food of the next?" Jesus said: "None of what you see is from the food of this world nor from the food of the next, but it is something God made by His lofty power. So eat of what you asked me for in the abode of this world, and I do not know what will become of you in the Hereafter."

Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb said: "You know what I want, and I do not know what you want."

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Yaḥyā said: "You know my secret, and I do not know your secret, because the secret is in its place, the souls."

Al-Zajjāj said: "He knows all that I know, and I do not know what He knows." Nafs (self) is an expression for the totality and reality of a thing, its essence. ﴿Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾ [Qur'an 5:116], what has been and what will be.

﴿I said to them only what You commanded me: "Worship God," my Lord and your Lord; and I was a witness over them while I remained among them. But when You caused me to die, You were the watcher over them﴾ [Qur'an 5:117], meaning: "I was a witness over them while I remained among them. But when You took me up, You were the one watching over them." ﴿When You took me to Yourself﴾, that is, took me back to You.

Al-Hasan said: Wafah (death, or taking back) in the Book of Allah occurs in three senses. The first is the wafah of death, as in ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ (39:42), meaning He completes their term. The second is the wafah of sleep, as in ﴿He it is who takes you back [in sleep] by night﴾ (6:60), meaning He puts you to sleep. The third is the wafah of raising, as in ﴿I will take you and raise you up﴾ (3:55).

﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants﴾ (5:118). Al-Hasan read: "fa-innahum ʿabīduka" (their servants) and "wa-in yatūbū fa-yaghfiru lahum" (and if they repent, He will forgive them), and "fa-innaka anta al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥakīm" (indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise).

Al-Suddi said: ﴿If You punish them﴾ means You cause them to die in their Christianity, ﴿indeed they are Your servants﴾. ﴿And if You forgive them﴾ means You bring them out of Christianity and guide them to Islam. ﴿Indeed You are the Lord, the Mighty, the Wise﴾: Mighty in dominion and vengeance, Wise in Your judgment.

Allah said: ﴿This is a day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness﴾ (5:119), in the Hereafter.

Qatadah said: The two speakers will speak on the Day of Resurrection, and that is what Allah has related to you. The enemy of Allah, Iblis, [will speak], as in His saying: ﴿And Satan will say when the matter has been decided﴾ (14:22). He led them astray from that on that day, and he had been a liar before, so his truthfulness did not benefit him that day. As for Jesus, he was truthful in life and after death, so his truthfulness benefited him.

ʿAtaʾ said: This is a day of the days of this world, because the Hereafter contains no action, only reward and recompense. The word "yawmu" is in the nominative as the predicate of "hadha" (this). Nafiʿ read it in the accusative according to the ḥarf (a reading variant), meaning: these things will occur on a day when ﴿the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness﴾. Al-Hasan read "hadha yawmun" with tanwin. Then Allah explained their reward, saying: ﴿For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is the great triumph﴾ (5:119). They attained Paradise and were saved from what they feared.

Then Allah exalted Himself above what the Christians said of falsehood, that He has a god with Him, saying: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, and He is over all things competent﴾ (5:120).

When God said, "O Jesus, son of Mary," meaning when God said, "O Jesus son of Mary." The position of ʿĪsā is accusative (naṣb) because it is a vocative (nidāʾ) if you treat the phrase as one vocative. If you prefer to make it two vocatives, then ʿĪsā is in the nominative (rafʿ) because it is a single, unmodified vocative, and "ibn" is in the accusative because it is a vocative with an attached noun. The sense of the sentence is "O Jesus, O son of Mary." Its parallel is the line of poetry:

*O Ḥakam ibn al-Mundhir ibn al-Jārūd,*
*you are the generous, son of the generous, son of generosity.* [[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 3/448.]]

This is under the same rule of nominative and accusative, and "ibn al-Mundhir" is not exempt from the accusative.

﴿Remember My favor upon you﴾. Al-Ḥasan said: Remembering a favor is giving thanks for it. By His words "My favor" He means "My favors," the word being singular in form but plural in meaning, as in His words: ﴿If you should count the favor of God, you could not enumerate it﴾ [Qur'an 14:34]. He means "the favors of God," because counting does not apply to a single favor. ﴿Upon you, O Jesus, and upon your mother, Mary.﴾ Then He mentions the favors: ﴿When I supported you with the Holy Spirit﴾, that is, I strengthened you and helped you with the Holy Spirit, meaning Jibrīl (Gabriel). ﴿You spoke to the people in the cradle and in maturity﴾, as a child and as a grown man, a prophet. ﴿And when I taught you the Book﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: God sent him when he was thirty years old, and he remained in his mission for thirty months, then God raised him to Himself. [Zad al-Masir of Ibn al-Jawzi: 1/332.]

﴿And the Book﴾ means writing (al-khaṭṭ), ﴿and wisdom﴾ means knowledge and understanding, ﴿and the Torah and the Gospel﴾. ﴿And when you shape from clay﴾, to make, form, depict and measure, up to His words ﴿So blessed is God, the best of creators﴾ [Qur'an 23:14], that is, the best of those who shape from clay, ﴿like the form of a bird﴾, like the image of a bird.

﴿By My permission, and you breathe into it, and it becomes a bird by My permission﴾, alive, flying by My permission. ﴿And you heal the blind and the leper by My permission﴾. ﴿And when you bring the dead out﴾ from their graves, alive, ﴿by My permission﴾. He revived Sām ibn Nūḥ, two men, a woman and a girl. ﴿And when I restrained the Children of Israel from you﴾, that is, the Jews, when they resolved to kill you. ﴿When you came to them with clear proofs﴾, meaning the signs and miracles I have mentioned. ﴿Those among them who disbelieved said: "This is nothing but evident magic"﴾ [Qur'an 5:110], meaning what came to them of clear proofs. Whoever reads "sāḥir" (magician) with an alif, the pronoun refers to Jesus, peace be upon him.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥamdūn, Makkī ibn ʿAbdān, Abū al-Azhar, from Asbāṭ, from Mujāhid ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmayr, who said: When God said to Jesus, "Remember My favor upon you," he wore wool and ate leaves, did not store anything for tomorrow, had no house that could be ruined, and no child that could die. Wherever night overtook him, he spent it there.

﴿And when I inspired the disciples﴾, that is, I caused them to know and cast inspiration into their hearts.
